facts.value: follows federal FLSA on rate/threshold (1.5x after 40 hrs/week; no daily overtime; no higher salary floor)
facts.summary: On the core overtime rate and hours threshold, Massachusetts follows the same standard as federal law: no daily overtime, and 1.5x the regular rate after 40 hours in a workweek, with no higher salary floor. Massachusetts's own overtime statute (M.G.L. c.151, s.1A) exempts MORE occupations than the FLSA does -- including restaurant, hotel/motel, gas-station, and other listed employees -- so a worker exempt under Massachusetts law may still be owed overtime under the more protective federal law where the employer is FLSA-covered. Where the Massachusetts statute does apply, a prevailing employee is entitled to mandatory treble damages plus attorneys' fees and costs -- a stronger remedy than the FLSA's own framework, but that is a penalty/remedy difference, not a different pay rate or hours threshold.
facts.notes: Corrects a prior note that mischaracterized MA's exemption list as 'narrower' than federal's: s.1A actually exempts more occupations than the FLSA (verified directly against the statute text at malegislature.gov 2026-08-08) -- e.g. restaurant, hotel/motel, gasoline-station, and agricultural employees are exempt under MA law but may still be FLSA-covered. So on this rate/threshold fact, MA provides no overtime protection beyond federal; the treble-damages remedy (s.1B) is a separate, real, state-specific enhancement when the state statute itself applies. VERIFY periodically for amendments to the s.1A exemption list.

facts.summary: Massachusetts's minimum wage is $15.00 per hour, well above the federal $7.25.
facts.notes: $15.00 has been the rate since Jan 1, 2023 and no statutory increase is scheduled for 2026. Statute also requires the state rate stay at least $0.50 above the federal minimum. Verify no new legislation (e.g. pending S.1349) took effect.

facts.summary: Tipped employees may be paid a service rate of at least $6.75/hour, provided tips bring total pay to at least the $15.00 minimum wage.
facts.notes: Employer must make up the difference if tips plus service rate fall short of the full minimum wage.

facts.summary: Beyond the federal categories, Massachusetts's fair employment law expressly protects sexual orientation, gender identity, ancestry, genetic information, pregnancy-related conditions, and veteran/military status.
facts.notes: Also covers the federal classes (race, color, religion, national origin, sex, age, disability). Enforced by the MCAD.

facts.summary: Massachusetts anti-discrimination law covers employers with 6 or more employees, a lower threshold than the federal 15 (Title VII/ADA) or 20 (ADEA).
facts.notes: Statute defines 'employer' to exclude those with fewer than six persons in their employ.

facts.value: reasonable accommodation required for qualified handicapped persons
facts.summary: Chapter 151B requires employers to provide reasonable accommodation to a qualified person with a handicap who can perform the essential job functions, unless it would impose undue hardship.
facts.notes: Parallels the federal ADA duty but applies at the lower 6-employee coverage threshold. Chapter 151B also mandates reasonable accommodation for religious creed/observance.

facts.summary: A discrimination complaint must be filed with the MCAD within 300 days of the alleged discriminatory act.
facts.notes: Limited case-by-case exceptions (e.g., equitable tolling) may extend the deadline.

facts.value: 3 years for general Wage Act claims; 2 years for the overtime-premium portion of an overtime claim
facts.summary: A civil action for unpaid wages under the Massachusetts Wage Act (e.g., late/unpaid regular wages, unlawful deductions, late final pay) must be brought within 3 years of the violation. Massachusetts's separate overtime statute has its own, shorter 2-year limitations period for the overtime-premium portion of an unpaid-overtime claim. An employee whose overtime-premium claim is more than 2 years old may still be able to recover the straight-time (regular-rate) value of the unpaid hours for a 3rd year under the Wage Act, but not the extra overtime premium for that additional year.
facts.citation: M.G.L. c. 151, s. 20A (overtime claims, 2 years); M.G.L. c. 149, s. 150 (general Wage Act claims, 3 years); Crocker v. Townsend Oil Co., Inc., 464 Mass. 1 (2012)
facts.notes: CORRECTED 2026-08-10: the prior version of this fact cited only c.149 s.150 (3 years) as the limitations period for 'unpaid wages or overtime.' But s.150's own enumerated list of sections eligible for a private civil action (ss. 33E, 52E, 148, 148A, 148B, 148C, 150C, 152, 152A, 159C, 190, and c.151 s.19) does NOT include c.151 ss.1A/1B -- the overtime-rate and overtime-violation sections -- confirmed against the statute text at malegislature.gov. Massachusetts's overtime statute carries its own limitations provision, c.151 s.20A, barring any cause of action accruing more than 2 years before filing (tolled while a complaint is pending with the Attorney General, same mechanism as s.150). The Supreme Judicial Court's decision in Crocker v. Townsend Oil Co., Inc., 464 Mass. 1 (2012), confirmed the 2-year period for the overtime-premium claim under s.20A, while holding an employee can still reach a 3rd year of straight-time-only recovery via the Wage Act (c.149 ss.148/150). So: general Wage Act claims = 3 years (c.149 s.150); the overtime-premium claim specifically = 2 years (c.151 s.20A). The 2-year figure in s.20A is corroborated by multiple secondary sources describing the Crocker holding but should be re-confirmed against the enrolled statute text directly before counsel review, since the malegislature.gov page for s.20A is JavaScript-rendered and returned inconsistent automated extracts during this pass. VERIFY periodically for amendment.

facts.value: public employees protected under c.149 s.185; wage-complaint retaliation barred for all employees under c.149 s.148A
facts.summary: Massachusetts's general whistleblower statute protects public employees who report legal, health, safety, or environmental violations; separately, retaliation against any employee for asserting Wage Act rights is prohibited.
facts.citation: M.G.L. c. 149, s. 185 (public employees); M.G.L. c. 149, s. 148A (wage retaliation)
facts.notes: The general whistleblower statute (s.185) applies only to public-sector employers. Private-sector wage/overtime retaliation is covered by c.149 s.148A.

facts.value: discharge: same day; resignation: next regular payday (or following Saturday if none)
facts.summary: Massachusetts requires an employee who is discharged to be paid in full on the day of discharge; an employee who resigns must be paid in full on the next regular payday, or the following Saturday if there is no regular payday.
facts.notes: Confirmed directly against the primary statute text, fetched from malegislature.gov. Massachusetts's same-day-of-discharge rule is unusually strict; violations of the Wage Act carry mandatory treble damages, attorney's fees, and costs (see deadlines.wageClaim, above).
